title: Zhipu opens GLM-5.3-FlashX at 200 tokens per second on 100,000 domestic chips
subtitle: The new accelerated variant of GLM-5.3-Flash lifts inference from 30–50 tokens per second to a maximum of 200, without changing the underlying model, and demonstrates production throughput on non-Nvidia silicon.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Zhipu launched GLM-5.3-FlashX on September 18, an accelerated variant of GLM-5.3-Flash that lifts maximum output speed from 30–50 tokens per second to 200. The underlying model is unchanged — 320 billion total parameters, 18 billion activated, native multimodal, 1 million token context — and the pricing sits at 2 RMB per million input tokens and 7 RMB per million output tokens, above standard Flash but well below the flagship GLM-5.3. Zhipu credited the speedup to inference capacity from roughly 100,000 domestic AI accelerators plus infra and serving optimization, and said throughput has tripled in under two weeks.

The story is not the tokens per second. It is the substrate. FlashX runs on Chinese-made accelerators — Huawei Ascend and adjacent silicon — at a per-token cost Zhipu claims is comparable to mainstream Nvidia deployments. For two years the answer to 'can Chinese chips serve frontier inference at scale?' has been 'in theory' or 'in benchmarks.' A five- to six-fold speedup on a live, paid API tier, sold at published prices, is a different kind of answer.

Context: this comes alongside Huawei's Ascend 960 Superpod announcement earlier this week and the Shanghai AI Lab's Atria Dawn 744B agentic MoE. Domestic Chinese labs are stitching together a full stack — chips, interconnect, model, serving — that no longer needs Nvidia in the critical path for inference workloads. Training is still the harder problem, and export-controlled HBM remains a chokepoint. But if Zhipu can hold 200 tokens per second for a 320B MoE on 100,000 domestic accelerators through October, the argument that Chinese frontier inference is compute-bound stops being credible.

Takeaway for learners — inference economics are becoming a national-industrial story, not just a model story. When you compare providers in 2026, look at three numbers together: tokens per second, price per million tokens, and the substrate the model is served on. A cheap model on scarce chips is a marketing headline; a fast model on a supply chain the vendor controls is a business. The interesting AI infrastructure to study for the next year is not the model at the top of the leaderboard — it is the stack underneath the model that keeps shipping when the export controls change.
